wcag-principles.text: The senior tell: automated scanners (axe, Lighthouse) catch only a subset of WCAG issues — estimates range from roughly a third to about half — the machine-checkable ones like missing alt text, contrast, and absent labels. They cannot judge whether focus order is logical, whether an error message actually helps, or whether alt text is meaningful. WCAG 2.1 AA is the legal bar most regulations currently point to (ADA Title II, EN 301 549 v3.2.1, the European Accessibility Act); WCAG 2.2 is the newer W3C version but not yet the referenced legal standard. 'The scan is green' is where the audit starts, not where it ends.

wcag-principles.question: Your reviewer says: 'axe reports zero violations on this checkout — prove it's actually accessible.' What is the strongest response?
options: Re-run axe and show the green result again — a passing automated scan is conformance.
Attach the axe pass PLUS a keyboard-only walkthrough (every step reachable, focus visible, no trap) and a screen-reader smoke pass showing errors are announced with a suggested fix.
Point out that the design matches the approved Figma mockup exactly.
Explain that no users have complained yet, so it must be fine.

keyboard-and-screen-reader-flows.text: The demo looks flawless on the projector — until QA unplugs the mouse. Tab, tab, tab: focus vanishes into the void behind an open modal, the inline error nobody heard fires silently, and a keyboard user is now stranded on a screen they cannot escape or complete.

A polished visual is only half the interface; the other half is the invisible path a keyboard and a screen reader trace through it. This flow is Section 1 of the accessibility packet you carry through the rest of Module 4 — the artifact that proves the screen works when nobody is looking at it.

Accessibility is a flow, not a snapshot; the scan grades the snapshot.

keyboard-and-screen-reader-flows.code:
## 1. Keyboard & Screen Reader Flow — checkout form
### Focus order (Tab)
| # | element        | role        | announced name + state                    |
|---|----------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Email input    | textbox     | "Email, edit text, required"              |
| 2 | Add coupon     | button      | "Add coupon, button, collapsed"           |
| 3 | Pay $42        | button      | "Pay 42 dollars, button"                  |
### Focus MOVES on state change
- open modal   -> focus first field; page behind is inert (aria-hidden), focus trapped
- close/esc    -> focus returns to the trigger that opened it
- submit valid -> focus Confirmation (role=status): "Payment confirmed"
- submit error -> focus Error summary (role=alert): "2 problems. Email is required."
### State matrix (each MUST announce)
- loading  -> button aria-busy; "Submitting, please wait"
- empty    -> "No saved cards. Add a card to continue."
- error    -> role=alert names the count + first field + how to fix
- disabled -> aria-disabled + reason, never a dead silent control
- success  -> role=status, focus moved so it is heard, not just seen
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.

Focus order is a contract: Every stop names role AND state. 'Add coupon, button, collapsed' proves aria-expanded is wired — a screen-reader user must hear whether it is open or closed before deciding to activate it.

Trap and return focus: A modal that does not trap focus lets Tab wander into the dimmed page behind it — the single most common keyboard failure. Esc and close must return focus to the trigger, or the user is dumped at the top of the document.
Success must MOVE focus: A confirmation that only appears visually is silent to a screen reader. Move focus to a role=status region so the change is announced, not just painted.

The error is the hard case: role=alert announces immediately; it names how many problems, the first offending field, and how to fix it — and offers a link that jumps focus straight to that field. This is the error-recovery the source scenario demands.

Every state announces: loading, empty, error, disabled, success — each has an announcement, so system status is never hidden. 'Looks polished but the user cannot tell what happened' is exactly the failure this matrix prevents.
Change one user, state, hierarchy, accessibility, or evidence constraint and identify the required repair.

# 4. Submit valid: focus moves to a role=status confirmation so the success is announced, not just painted. Run one screen-reader smoke pass to hear it.

storyboard.say: Start at the entry: focus lands on the email field, and the cart summary sits deliberately outside the tab loop.
Tab moves focus forward: email to the add-coupon button, then onward to the pay button. Every stop is reachable and visible.
The pay button is the decision point. Submit branches two ways, and both branches must force focus somewhere and announce it.
On invalid, code must MOVE focus to the error summary and announce it — name, role, state — so a screen reader user hears the failure.
Recovery: the error summary links straight to the offending field, so the user jumps back and fixes it instead of hunting.
On valid, code MOVES focus to the confirmation and announces success — the repair path that completes the flow.
The invariant: for every state change, name where focus goes and what is announced. No state may leave focus lost.

keyboard-and-screen-reader-flows.code:
## 1. Keyboard & Screen Reader Flow — checkout form
### Focus order (Tab)
| # | element        | role        | announced name + state                    |
|---|----------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Email input    | textbox     | "Email, edit text, required"              |
| 2 | Add coupon     | button      | "Add coupon, button, collapsed"           |
| 3 | Pay $42        | button      | "Pay 42 dollars, button"                  |
### Focus MOVES on state change
- open modal   -> focus first field; page behind is inert (aria-hidden), focus trapped
- close/esc    -> focus returns to the trigger that opened it
- submit valid -> focus Confirmation (role=status): "Payment confirmed"
- submit error -> focus Error summary (role=alert): "2 problems. Email is required."
### State matrix (each MUST announce)
- loading  -> button aria-busy; "Submitting, please wait"
- empty    -> "No saved cards. Add a card to continue."
- error    -> role=alert names the count + first field + how to fix
- disabled -> aria-disabled + reason, never a dead silent control
- success  -> role=status, focus moved so it is heard, not just seen

steps.label: Focus order is a contract
steps.note: Every stop names role AND state. 'Add coupon, button, collapsed' proves aria-expanded is wired — a screen-reader user must hear whether it is open or closed before deciding to activate it.

steps.label: Trap and return focus
steps.note: A modal that does not trap focus lets Tab wander into the dimmed page behind it — the single most common keyboard failure. Esc and close must return focus to the trigger, or the user is dumped at the top of the document.

steps.label: Success must MOVE focus
steps.note: A confirmation that only appears visually is silent to a screen reader. Move focus to a role=status region so the change is announced, not just painted.

steps.label: The error is the hard case
steps.note: role=alert announces immediately; it names how many problems, the first offending field, and how to fix it — and offers a link that jumps focus straight to that field. This is the error-recovery the source scenario demands.

steps.label: Every state announces
steps.note: loading, empty, error, disabled, success — each has an announcement, so system status is never hidden. 'Looks polished but the user cannot tell what happened' is exactly the failure this matrix prevents.

keyboard-and-screen-reader-flows.text: The pro move that separates a real audit from a checkbox: run the flow with the mouse unplugged AND the screen reader on, at the same time. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order), 2.4.7 (Focus Visible), 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 4.1.3 (Status Messages) are all about behavior, not markup — axe can pass every one of them while the flow is unusable. keyboard-and-screen-reader-flows.question: A reviewer challenges: "Prove this checkout is accessible, not just described." Which evidence actually proves the flow works?
options: An axe scan report showing zero violations across every screen state.
A keyboard-only walkthrough recording plus the focus-order table, showing focus moving to the role=alert error summary on invalid submit and returning to the trigger when the modal closes.
A note that every input has a visible label and passes color-contrast.
A screenshot of the finished, visually-polished confirmation screen.

The axe scan (1) and the label/contrast note (3) grade the static snapshot and miss lost focus and silent errors; the screenshot (4) proves the visual, which was never the doubt. The reviewer's challenge is exactly 'usable, not just understood' — a walkthrough is the inspectable artifact that answers it.

usability-test-plan.unlock: Your plan names a measurable task, a leading-indicator metric, a falsifiable failure, and a non-leading prompt — and a peer could run it without you in the room.
usability-test-plan.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a usability test plan if your prompt tells the user what to click ("now press the blue Submit button"). That measures your narration, not their comprehension. And do not claim a screen is tested because it "looks polished" — polish is not evidence; a completed task under observation is.

usability-test-plan.text: The demo looks flawless — until you hand the laptop to a real user and they freeze on the checkout screen, thumb hovering, whispering "wait, did that save?" Nobody in the room framed the question that would have caught it: can a stranger finish this, recover from a mistake, and do it with a keyboard and a screen reader?

You already have a journey map, wireframe, and WCAG checklist from earlier in this module — but a polished artifact that no one watched a user attempt is untested confidence. The usability test plan is the operational-evidence layer: it turns "unclear state, weak feedback, inaccessible interactions" into a script that produces observable proof another reviewer can inspect.

usability-test-plan.prompt: You want to test your new signup flow. Your plan says: "Ask the user if they found the form easy to use." What is wrong with that as a test? Answer before reading on.
usability-test-plan.reveal: It measures a feeling after the fact, not behavior during the task — and it is leading ("easy" plants the answer). People say "yes, easy" and then fail. A real plan gives a goal-level task ("Create an account and add a payment method"), then stays silent and records what they actually do: where they hesitate, what they misread, whether they recover from the error, whether the keyboard and screen reader can complete it. You test the workflow, not the opinion.

usability-test-plan.code:
# Usability Test Plan — Checkout flow
## 1. Task (goal-level, non-leading)
"You want to buy the item in your cart. Complete the purchase and add a new card."
## 2. Constraint
Must be completable keyboard-only AND with VoiceOver; primary conversion path — no dead ends.
## 3. Success metric
Task completion (yes/no) + error-recovery (recovers unaided?) + time-to-first-action.
## 4. State matrix to observe
loading | empty-cart | field-error | disabled-submit | success-confirmation
## 5. Failure I fear
After a declined card, status is silent — user cannot tell if it charged, retries, double-pays.
## 6. Inspection hooks used
axe accessibility scan + keyboard-only walkthrough + screen-reader smoke pass
## 7. Before / after critique
Before: submit spinner never resolves on decline. After: inline error + "card not charged" status.
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.

The task line: Goal-level and non-leading. It names the user's intent ("buy the item", "add a card"), never a UI element. If it says "click Submit", you scripted the answer and the test measures nothing.
The constraint: Keyboard-only AND screen-reader, on the primary conversion path. This is the non-negotiable that rules out "looks fine on my mouse" as proof.
The metric: Completion is the headline, but recovery and time-to-first-action are the leading indicators that catch unclear state before completion even fails.
The state matrix: Every state a real workflow passes through. Untested empty/error/disabled states are where polished screens quietly break.
The feared failure: Specific enough to recognize live: silent status after a decline. Naming it makes the test falsifiable — you know exactly what a failing run looks like.
Before/after critique: The repair, made inspectable. A reviewer replays the decline path and sees status went from silent spinner to explicit "card not charged".
Change one user, state, hierarchy, accessibility, or evidence constraint and identify the required repair.

storyboard.say: A usability test starts here: a single task prompt you read once, then stay silent. Naming the UI would be narration, not a test.
The participant attempts the real workflow while you record behavior, not opinions. You watch what their hands actually do.
Every action is judged against the state matrix. This is the decision point where the test either passes or exposes a gap.
The failure path: the user hits an ambiguous state, freezes on checkout whispering 'did that save?', and the task stalls.
The recovered path: status is visible, feedback is clear, and the participant finishes. Completion gets logged as proof.
Both branches converge on the evidence packet. Even a stalled task fires a metric that logs the failure for review.
The insight: this flow turns polished but untested confidence into observable proof another reviewer can inspect.

# Usability Test Plan — Checkout flow
## 1. Task (goal-level, non-leading)
"You want to buy the item in your cart. Complete the purchase and add a new card."
## 2. Constraint
Must be completable keyboard-only AND with VoiceOver; primary conversion path — no dead ends.
## 3. Success metric
Task completion (yes/no) + error-recovery (recovers unaided?) + time-to-first-action.
## 4. State matrix to observe
loading | empty-cart | field-error | disabled-submit | success-confirmation
## 5. Failure I fear
After a declined card, status is silent — user cannot tell if it charged, retries, double-pays.
## 6. Inspection hooks used
axe accessibility scan + keyboard-only walkthrough + screen-reader smoke pass
## 7. Before / after critique
Before: submit spinner never resolves on decline. After: inline error + "card not charged" status.

steps.label: The task line
steps.note: Goal-level and non-leading. It names the user's intent ("buy the item", "add a card"), never a UI element. If it says "click Submit", you scripted the answer and the test measures nothing.

steps.label: The constraint
steps.note: Keyboard-only AND screen-reader, on the primary conversion path. This is the non-negotiable that rules out "looks fine on my mouse" as proof.

steps.label: The metric
steps.note: Completion is the headline, but recovery and time-to-first-action are the leading indicators that catch unclear state before completion even fails.

steps.label: The state matrix
steps.note: Every state a real workflow passes through. Untested empty/error/disabled states are where polished screens quietly break.

steps.label: The feared failure
steps.note: Specific enough to recognize live: silent status after a decline. Naming it makes the test falsifiable — you know exactly what a failing run looks like.

steps.label: Before/after critique
steps.note: The repair, made inspectable. A reviewer replays the decline path and sees status went from silent spinner to explicit "card not charged".

usability-test-plan.text: The senior tell is silence. Amateurs coach the participant ("you probably want the menu up top") and record their own hints as user success. A pro reads the task once, then shuts up — because every word after the prompt contaminates the evidence. Nielsen's heuristic "visibility of system status" is exactly what that silence reveals: if the user has to ask you "did it work?", the interface failed, not the participant.

usability-test-plan.question: A reviewer challenges: "Prove this usability test plan is real, not just described." Which artifact answers the challenge?
options: A slide saying the team ran usability testing and users were satisfied.
A plan with a goal-level task, a state matrix, a completion + recovery metric, one non-leading prompt, and before/after notes showing the silent-decline failure was found and repaired.
A polished high-fidelity mockup of the final screen.
A list of usability best practices the design follows.
usability-test-plan.explanation: Only option 2 is inspectable and falsifiable: a reviewer can read the exact prompt (and confirm it does not lead), replay the state matrix, check the metric fired, and see the failure was caught and repaired. Satisfaction slides (1), mockups (3), and best-practice lists (4) all describe the design — none let a reviewer replay a user's failure or verify task completion improved.

usability-test-plan.intro: Prove your test plan holds — no vibes:
items: Read your task prompt aloud. If it names a UI element (button, menu, tab) or a verb like "click", it is narration — rewrite it at the goal level ("complete the purchase").
Confirm your success metric is a behavior you can observe live (completed? recovered from the error unaided? time to first action?) — not a post-hoc opinion.
Check the state matrix covers loading, empty, error, disabled, and success — the states where polished screens silently break.
Confirm the plan requires a keyboard-only pass AND a screen-reader smoke pass, plus one axe scan — not just a mouse walkthrough.
Name the exact failure you fear (e.g. silent status after a decline) and confirm a failing run is recognizable — if you cannot describe a fail, the test cannot pass either.
Hand the plan to a peer: could they run the session and score it without you in the room? If not, it is a note, not a plan.

critique-loop.unlock: Your packet shows the constraint, the failure path AND the repair path, at least two inspection-hook outputs (axe scan, keyboard walkthrough, screen-reader smoke, or usability note), and a transfer case that changes the environment — not just the wording.
critique-loop.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'ran a critique' if you only listed heuristics that sound correct. A critique with no failure trigger, no rejected option, and no statement of what evidence would change the decision is decoration. The loop is proven only when the weak version is broken on purpose and the repair is shown.

critique-loop.text: The demo looks flawless: crisp cards, tasteful spacing, a confident CTA. Then a keyboard-only user tabs in, the focus ring vanishes into a modal, the form rejects their input with no message, and they are stranded — and everyone in the room realizes the polish was hiding a flow nobody could actually complete.

A high-friction workflow becomes shippable only when it is understandable, accessible, and measurable — not when it looks finished. The critique loop is the release gate: it turns 'the interface looks polished' into inspectable proof that a real user can predict the next action, recover from an error, and finish with assistive tech.

critique-loop.prompt: A reviewer says your checkout screen 'looks clean and accessible.' Before you accept that — what is wrong with 'it looks accessible' as a verdict? Answer before reading on.
critique-loop.reveal: 'Looks accessible' is a visual judgment about a non-visual property. Accessibility lives in focus order, labels, name/role/value, error recovery, and contrast — none of which are visible in a static mockup. The critique-loop failure this lesson exists to kill: a design that passes the eye and fails the keyboard, the screen reader, and the empty/error states. A verdict you cannot replay with an axe scan or a keyboard walkthrough is an opinion, not a review.

# UX State, Accessibility & Review Packet — Checkout: Address Step
## 1. Constraint
- Users must complete address entry keyboard-only AND with a screen reader; WCAG 2.2 AA; no daytime deploy freeze.
## 2. Selected approach
- Inline validation on blur + aria-live="assertive" error summary; focus moves to first invalid field on submit.
## 3. Rejected approach
- Toast-only error ("Something went wrong"). Rejected: invisible to SR after it dismisses; no field association; no recovery.
## 4. Interaction states (matrix)
- loading: submit disabled + spinner + aria-busy | empty: helper text, no red | error: inline msg + aria-describedby | disabled: aria-disabled + reason | success: confirmed, focus to next step
## 5. Expected failure (break the weak version)
- Weak: error rendered as color-only red border, no text, focus stays on submit. Keyboard/SR user hears nothing, cannot find the bad field.
## 6. Verification (inspection hooks)
- axe scan: 0 serious/critical (was 3: label, name-role-value, contrast)
- keyboard walkthrough: Tab order = name→street→city→zip→submit; focus visible at each stop
- SR smoke (VoiceOver): error summary announced; each field name+error read on focus
## 7. Before/after critique
- Before: color-only error, focus trapped on submit, empty state looked like an error.
- After: text+icon+color error, focus jumps to first invalid field, empty state neutral. Task completion 62%→94% in 5-user test.
## 8. Reviewer objection + response
- Objection: "Is recovery proven or described?" Response: attached SR transcript + keyboard capture show a user recover from a bad ZIP without a mouse.
## 9. Usability-test prompt
- "Enter a shipping address using only your keyboard; if you make a mistake, fix it."
## 10. Transfer + capstone connection
- Reused as the accessibility evidence in the capstone flow packet.
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.
Constraint before fix: Name the non-negotiable first — keyboard AND screen reader, WCAG 2.2 AA. If a fix appears before the constraint, you pre-decided the review.
Selected + rejected: Record the rejected option (toast-only) and WHY it fails under this constraint. A packet with no rejected option hides the judgment.
State matrix — the states that get skipped: loading, empty, error, disabled, success. Empty ≠ error is the most-missed distinction; a neutral empty state stops users reading calm as failure.
Break the weak version: Color-only error + focus stuck on submit. This is the realistic failure: it passes the eye and fails the keyboard and the screen reader.
Prove with hooks (replayable): axe = 0 serious/critical, keyboard = named tab order, SR = announced error. Each is an output another reviewer can re-run — not a claim.
Before/after + the metric: 62%→94% task completion is the signal that the loop improved recovery, not just contrast. The metric hypothesis is part of the proof.
Objection response = evidence, not prose: 'Is recovery proven or merely described?' is answered with an SR transcript + keyboard capture — the exact reviewer challenge, met with an artifact.
Change one user, state, hierarchy, accessibility, or evidence constraint and identify the required repair.

A reviewer can point to the exact evidence that the design improves task completion, comprehension, and recovery.

critique-loop.title: The critique loop as a review circuit
critique-loop.subtitle: A polished-looking flow enters; each hook is a kill-test that can fail. The failure path (hidden status, dead-end error, broken focus) feeds the repair; PROVE re-runs the hooks. Only a replayable pass exits to release.

nodes.description: axe scan · keyboard walkthrough · SR smoke · usability note

nodes.label: Failure path
nodes.description: hidden status · dead-end error · broken focus order

nodes.description: live region · inline recovery · logical focus

legend.label: constraint + hooks that gate the review

storyboard.say: A polished-looking flow enters the review circuit — crisp cards, tasteful spacing, a confident CTA. But looks are not proof.
First, name the constraint. Before any fix, the review is bounded by what a real user must be able to do.
The constraint feeds the inspection hooks — each hook is a kill-test: keyboard focus, visible status, recoverable errors.
When a hook says 'no' — focus vanishes into a modal, a form rejects input silently — the flow drops onto the failure path.
The failure isn't a dead end; it's a diagnosis. The broken case routes into repair to fix the weak version.
Repair doesn't get to self-certify. It must PROVE the fix by re-running the exact same hooks.
Still failing? Prove loops straight back to the hooks — no escaping the gate until the evidence holds.
Only a replayable pass exits to release. The invariant: proof is replayable, or it never happened.

critique-loop.caption: The tell is not how it looks — it is whether the reviewer can re-run a hook and reproduce your verdict. Color-only error is the classic 'looks accessible, isn't' trap.

critique-loop.text: Standards grounding: WCAG 2.2 AA does the arguing for you. 'Error is color-only' isn't taste — it fails SC 1.4.1 (Use of Color) and 3.3.1 (Error Identification); a missing field name fails 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value); a lost focus ring fails 2.4.7 (Focus Visible). Cite the success criterion and your critique stops being an opinion and becomes a defect a reviewer must sign.

critique-loop.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Show me the exact evidence that this flow's error recovery is proven, not just described.' Which response actually closes the loop?
options: "I followed the heuristics and the design looks accessible — the error states are all styled."
A before/after packet with an axe scan (0 serious/critical), a named keyboard tab order, a screen-reader transcript announcing the error, and a 5-user task-completion delta (62%→94%).
"We added a red border and a toast, which is standard practice for forms."
A high-fidelity mockup showing the error state in the design tool.
critique-loop.explanation: Only option 2 is replayable proof: another reviewer can re-run the axe scan, re-trace the tab order, replay the SR transcript, and check the metric. prototype-to-code-handoff.text: The Figma looks flawless in the review, everyone claps, it ships — and two weeks later support is flooded: users hit submit twice because there was no disabled state, a blank screen looks broken because nobody designed the empty state, and a screen-reader user cannot tell the form failed. The prototype was perfect. The handoff was empty.

A prototype communicates one frame; a product lives in states. Prototype-to-code handoff is where you either specify every state and its accessibility contract, or you silently delegate those decisions to whoever writes the code under deadline — this is the first lesson of Implementation and Measurement because a design is only real once it survives being built.

prototype-to-code-handoff.prompt: You hand an engineer a pixel-perfect mockup of a 'Save changes' form. Which part of the real interface did you almost certainly NOT hand them? Answer before reading on.
prototype-to-code-handoff.reveal: Every state that isn't the success state. Your mockup showed the form full and valid — but not the loading spinner on submit, the empty state before data loads, the error state when the API 500s, the disabled state while the request is in flight, or how a screen reader announces any of it. Those four states are ~80% of the code and 100% of the support tickets, and a single-frame prototype specifies none of them. The mockup felt like a spec because it was polished; polish is not coverage.

# Handoff Packet — "Save address" form (checkout, step 2 of 3)

## Context
- Flow: guest checkout, high friction, unclear system state on submit
- Constraint: primary conversion path — no full-screen blocking, WCAG 2.2 AA

## State matrix (the deliverable)
| state    | trigger                    | UI                              | a11y contract                                              |
|----------|----------------------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| empty    | no saved address on load   | inline prompt + skeleton fields | focus lands on first field; label tied via for/id          |
| loading  | submit pressed             | button spinner, fields disabled | aria-busy=true; announce "Saving address…" (polite)        |
| disabled | request in flight          | button disabled, not removed    | aria-disabled; keep in tab order so focus is not lost      |
| error    | 422 / network fail         | inline error above the field    | role=alert (assertive); focus moves to error summary       |
| success  | 200                        | check + "Saved", advance CTA    | announce "Address saved"; move focus to next-step CTA      |

## Rejected approach
- Toast-only errors: vanish before AT users hear them; fail 3.3.1

## Metric hypothesis
- Defining empty+error states raises step-2 completion +?%, cuts double-submit

## Verification hooks used
- keyboard-only walkthrough  ·  axe accessibility scan  ·  screen-reader smoke pass
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.
Anchor the scenario: Name the exact surface, the flow it lives in, and the hard constraint (conversion path, WCAG 2.2 AA). The constraint rules options out — toast-only errors die here.
The state matrix is the artifact: Not a mockup — a table. One row per interaction state. If a row is missing, that state is being handed to the engineer's imagination.
Empty and loading first: The states a happy-path prototype never shows. Empty explains 'no data yet' so a blank screen doesn't read as broken; loading proves the system heard the click.
Disabled, not removed: Keep the button in the tab order (aria-disabled), don't yank it from the DOM — removing it drops keyboard focus into the void. This is the tell of a real a11y contract.
Error must be announced AND focused: role=alert makes a screen reader speak it; moving focus to the error summary makes recovery possible. Silent error = the flow the AT user cannot complete.

Name the rejected option: Toast-only errors risk failing WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA) — a status message that vanishes may not be programmatically exposed for assistive tech to announce (and if it's a detected input error, it must also be identified in text per 3.3.1, Level A). Recording the reject stops the engineer re-proposing it.
A metric, so 'better' is falsifiable: State the behavior the change should move — step-2 completion, double-submit rate. Without it, 'we improved the UX' can never be proven or disproven.
Change one user, state, hierarchy, accessibility, or evidence constraint and identify the required repair.

# 1. Name the user, trigger, goal, context, and evidence before proposing a surface.
# 2. Enumerate loading, empty, error, success, denied, destructive, responsive, keyboard, and screen-reader states.

storyboard.say: It starts with one perfect prototype frame — flawless in review, everyone claps. But a frame is a single moment, not a living product.
The real handoff expands that one frame into an inventory of every state the product can actually enter.
Enumerate them all: loading, empty, error, disabled, success — five interaction states the frame never showed you.
Each state binds to an accessibility contract: focus order, labels, contrast, and what the screen reader announces.
Now it's a buildable spec — the engineer codes the screen from explicit contracts, then instruments a metric to prove it works.
Here is the failure path: any state left undefined doesn't vanish — it becomes the engineer's guess under deadline.
That guess leaks straight into what ships: no disabled state, a blank empty screen, a form a screen reader can't announce.
The invariant: an undefined state is a state the engineer invents — so specify every state, or delegate the design by accident.

instrumentation-plan.prompt: You redesign a signup form to reduce friction and add one event: 'signup_completed'. Two weeks later completions are flat. Can you tell whether the redesign worked? Answer before reading on.
instrumentation-plan.reveal: No — a single success event measures the survivors, never the failure behavior. Flat completions could mean the redesign did nothing, OR it fixed the form for keyboard users while a new inline-validation bug traps screen-reader users at the same rate. Without events on the empty, error, and abandon states, you cannot separate 'no effect' from 'two opposite effects cancelling out'. Instrumentation is measuring where users get STUCK, not only where they arrive.

instrumentation-plan.code:
## Instrumentation Plan
# Behavior hypothesis (falsifiable, with a number):
#   "Inline validation + clearer state raises 3-step signup completion
#    from 61% to >=68% within 14 days, WITHOUT raising median time-to-complete."

# Event schema (one row per STATE, not per screen):
#   form_step_viewed   { step:int, flow_id, variant }         trigger: step renders
#   field_error        { field, code, a11y_announced:bool }   trigger: validation fails
#   flow_abandoned     { last_step, had_error:bool }          trigger: exit w/o complete
#   flow_completed     { duration_ms, errors_seen:int }       trigger: success screen

# Guardrail (must NOT regress):  median duration_ms  AND  field_error rate for
#   screen-reader sessions (a11y_announced=true) — polish can hide new a11y traps

# Read rule (stop + decide):  read at n>=2000 completed flows OR day 14;
#   ship if completion +>=7pts AND guardrails flat; else roll back + inspect field_error
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.

A falsifiable hypothesis: Names the behavior, the current baseline (61%), the target (68%), AND a guardrail clause. A hypothesis with no number and no 'without' clause cannot fail — so it can never pass.
form_step_viewed — the denominator: Fires per step, not per page load. Without a per-step viewed event you have no denominator, so 'completion rate' is a fraction with no bottom.

field_error — the failure signal: The property a11y_announced captures whether the error was actually surfaced to assistive tech. This is the event the vanity plan never adds — and the one that catches a polished-but-inaccessible flow.
flow_abandoned with had_error: had_error separates 'left because it was broken' from 'left for lunch'. Abandon without context is noise.
flow_completed — success WITH cost: errors_seen and duration_ms mean success is not binary: a flow people finish only after 3 errors is a warning, not a win.
The guardrail: Scoped to screen-reader sessions on purpose — the exact failure this course fears is a flow that looks better in aggregate while getting worse for assistive-tech users.
The read rule: A pre-committed n and decision. Deciding the threshold AFTER seeing the data is how teams talk themselves into shipping a regression.

legend.label: schema sink — versioned, out-of-scope noise excluded

storyboard.say: The flow starts here, and the very first thing it does is emit an event to the analytics sink — instrumentation begins before the user even types.
The user fills the form and submits, handing their input to the validation gate that decides what happens next.
This is the fork the whole lesson turns on: validation either passes to success or fails into an error state.
Both outcomes are named and measured — success emits to the sink, and crucially, so does the error state.
From the error, two human paths open: the user recovers back to input, or they give up and abandon the flow entirely.
The error event is the key signal — if the plan cannot fire this, the failure has no number and stays invisible for weeks.
That is the skill: instrument every state, guard the one that must not regress, and prove the failure so you can prove the fix.

metric-tree.unlock: Your tree roots at ONE outcome, decomposes into mechanically-connected drivers, grounds each driver in a real instrumented event, and separates what you observe from what you infer.
metric-tree.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a metric tree if it is just a dashboard of metrics side by side. A wall of KPIs with no parent-child causality is a scoreboard, not a tree. The tree's value is the EDGES — each child must plausibly move its parent, or it does not belong on this branch.

metric-tree.text: The redesign shipped, the screens look gorgeous, and the exec asks the one question that empties the room: "Did it work?" Nobody can answer, because "engagement is up" moved but activation, completion, and error-recovery — the things the redesign actually touched — were never wired to the outcome anyone cared about.

A polished flow that you cannot measure is a bet you placed blind: it may have helped task completion, hurt it, or done nothing, and you have no way to tell. The Metric Tree is the artifact that connects one outcome you care about to the specific interaction-level events your design changed — so "did it work?" becomes inspectable instead of a vibe.

metric-tree.prompt: You ship an accessibility + form-feedback overhaul and pick "weekly active users up 6%" as your proof it worked. Before you celebrate — what is wrong with that as the measure of success? Answer before reading on.
metric-tree.reveal: It is a north-star metric measuring a driver-level change — the causal chain is too long to be evidence. WAU moves with marketing, seasonality, a pricing email, ten things your redesign never touched. Your overhaul acted on error-recovery and task completion; those are the DRIVER metrics directly downstream of what you changed. A metric tree makes you name the child metric your work mechanically moves BEFORE you claim credit at the root — so success is attributable, not coincidental.

# Metric Tree — Checkout Redesign

## Root (north-star outcome)
- checkout_completion_rate = paid_sessions / sessions_with_intent   [observed]

## Drivers (each must mechanically move the root)
- D1 step1_activation   = form_reached / sessions_with_intent       [observed]
- D2 field_progression  = fields_passed / fields_entered            [observed]
- D3 error_recovery     = errors_corrected / errors_shown           [inferred: no announce event yet]

## Leaves (instrumented events under each driver)
- D1 <- form_first_focus        (focus enters first field)
- D2 <- field_valid_on_blur     (blur passes validation)
- D3 <- inline_error_shown      (error rendered AND aria-live announced)
- D3 <- error_corrected         (same field re-validates pass)

## Metric hypothesis (one, falsifiable)
- If inline+announced errors replace the submit-time error summary,
  error_recovery (D3) rises >= 15% and completion_rate rises,
  with NO drop in field_progression (D2).  Guardrail: D2 must not fall.

## Inspection hooks used
- keyboard-only walkthrough (confirmed focus lands on errored field)
- screen-reader smoke pass  (confirmed aria-live announces the error)
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.
The root is ONE outcome: A ratio, not a raw count — and it names its denominator (sessions_with_intent), so a reviewer knows exactly what population it measures. Tag it observed: you have the event.
Drivers must mechanically feed the root: Activation × progression × recovery is the actual mechanics of finishing checkout. If a metric here cannot move completion, it is off-tree.

Tag observed vs inferred — the honesty move: D3 is INFERRED because there is no announce event yet: you are computing recovery from a guess. Naming that is the difference between an inspectable tree and false confidence.
Leaves are real instrumented events: inline_error_shown fires only when the error is rendered AND announced via aria-live — the a11y requirement is baked into the event, not a footnote.
One falsifiable metric hypothesis: A direction (D3 up >=15%), a mechanism (announced inline errors), and a guardrail (D2 must not fall). A hypothesis with no guardrail hides the trade you just made.
Attach the inspection hooks: The keyboard + screen-reader passes are what let you claim the leaf event is real for assistive-tech users, not just mouse users.

# Novice workflow:
# 1. Name the user, trigger, goal, context, and evidence before proposing a surface.
# 2. Enumerate loading, empty, error, success, denied, destructive, responsive, keyboard, and screen-reader states.

storyboard.say: Start at the root: checkout completion rate is the one outcome we care about, the north star the whole tree exists to answer for.
One level down, three drivers mechanically feed that outcome: step-1 activation, field progression, and error recovery.
Each driver bottoms out in leaf events we actually instrument. form_first_focus measures whether users even start, feeding activation.
field_valid_on_blur measures whether users move cleanly through the form, feeding field progression.
Error recovery draws from two events: inline_error_shown when a problem surfaces, and error_corrected when the user fixes it.
Support tickets sit off the tree — correlated with checkout, but no causal edge the redesign can defend, so it stays disconnected.
The invariant: every edge is a causal claim. A child must move its parent or it's off-tree — that's what turns 'did it work?' into something inspectable.

design-review-packet.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) high-friction workflow you are about to ship and assemble a Design Review Packet: a journey/state inventory, the loading/empty/error/disabled/success states, WCAG notes for keyboard/screen-reader/contrast/labels/focus order, one before/after critique, and the release risk another reviewer can inspect.
design-review-packet.proof: The artifact ux_state_accessibility_and_review_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger: context, assumptions, selected approach, rejected approach, expected failure, verification method (2+ inspection hooks run), reviewer objection, and repair notes. A second reviewer can trace one request through the flow and tell whether it improves task completion, comprehension, and recovery.
design-review-packet.unlock: Your packet inventories every interaction state, carries a WCAG checklist with real hook output, and names the release/review risk with a repair — not just a polished screenshot.
design-review-packet.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a design review packet if it only shows the happy-path success screen. A packet that skips loading, empty, error, and disabled states, or that lists 'accessible' with no axe/keyboard/screen-reader output, is a demo — it looks reviewable and fails the moment release risk changes.

design-review-packet.text: The build is 'done,' the demo looks clean, and someone asks to ship it Friday — until a reviewer tabs into the form with a keyboard, hits an error, and lands nowhere, focus lost, no recovery, screen reader silent. The interface was polished; nobody had packaged the proof that a real user could finish.

This sits at the end of Implementation & Measurement: the flow is built, so the remaining risk is release/review risk. The Design Review Packet is the artifact that converts 'it looks finished' into an inspectable decision — every state, the accessibility trail, and the failure another reviewer can replay.

design-review-packet.prompt: A teammate shows you a beautiful implemented screen and says 'the checkout redesign is ready for review.' Before you approve — what is missing that makes 'ready' unprovable? Answer before reading on.
design-review-packet.reveal: A single polished screen is the success state — one of at least five. The packet's job is the other four: what shows while loading, what an empty result looks like, what happens on error (and how the user recovers), and what disabled means. Add the accessibility trail — keyboard path, focus order, screen-reader labels, contrast — and 'ready' becomes something a reviewer can inspect instead of admire. Polish hides the states where users actually get stuck.

design-review-packet.code:
# UX State, Accessibility & Review Packet

## Context
- Flow: submit an insurance claim (high-friction, multi-step form)
- Constraint: release risk — cannot ship a flow keyboard/SR users can't complete
- Assumption: most drop-off happens at the error + resubmit step

## State Inventory
| State     | System status shown | Primary action        | Notes |
|-----------|--------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| loading   | spinner + 'Saving' | none (disabled)       | aria-busy=true |
| empty     | 'No claims yet'    | 'Start a claim'       | first-run guidance |
| error     | field-level + banner | 'Fix & resubmit'    | focus moves to first error |
| disabled  | greyed, aria-disabled | tooltip 'why'       | reason is stated |
| success   | confirmation + ref# | 'View claim'         | the demoed screen |

## Accessibility (WCAG)
- [ ] keyboard-only: full flow reachable, no traps  (hook: keyboard-only walkthrough)
- [ ] focus order: DOM order matches visual order; error moves focus
- [ ] screen reader: labels + error text announced  (hook: screen-reader smoke pass)
- [ ] contrast: error red passes 4.5:1  (hook: axe accessibility scan)

## Selected vs Rejected
- Selected: inline field errors + focus-to-first-error
- Rejected: single top banner only — SR users never hear which field

## Expected Failure & Repair
- Failure: on submit error, focus stays on the button; SR user hears nothing
- Repair: move focus to first invalid field, aria-live=assertive on the summary

## Before/After Critique
- Before: error banner appears off-screen, no focus move, context lost
- After: focus + announcement + inline messages; recovery in one step

## Reviewer Objection
- 'Is this proven or just described?' -> attached axe report + keyboard GIF

## Evidence
- axe_scan.json · keyboard_walkthrough.md · usability_prompt.md
steps: Predict the critique result before executing.
Context + the real constraint: Name the flow and that the operating constraint is release/review risk — not aesthetics. State the assumption you're testing so a reviewer knows what to attack.
The state inventory: Every row is a state a demo skips. 'System status shown' is the heuristic that catches hidden loading/disabled states; the error row's focus-move note is the recovery hinge.
WCAG checklist with hooks named: Each line binds to a concrete inspection hook (axe scan, keyboard-only walkthrough, screen-reader smoke pass). A checkbox with no hook output is a wish, not proof.
Selected vs rejected: The rejected option (top-banner-only) is the one that looks acceptable in review and fails for screen-reader users — the exact invalidation condition.
Expected failure + repair: The realistic failure: focus stranded on the submit button after an error. The repair is specific and testable, not 'improve accessibility'.

design-review-packet.subtitle: One task (submit a claim) fans into five interaction states plus the accessibility layer that must hold across all of them. The polished demo is only the green node; the packet forces the warning and decision nodes into view — including the error → recovery path.

storyboard.say: One task drives everything: a user hits submit to file a claim, and the whole interaction begins.
That submit fans into three outcomes from loading — it resolves to success, returns no data, or fails outright.
The demo only ever shows the green success node — the clean happy path everyone signs off on.
But the packet forces the warning states into view: empty and error are real states a reviewer must be able to replay.
Error is the decision point — the interface must offer a way out, not strand the user with focus lost.
Recovery loops back to the task with context intact, so retry doesn't mean starting over.
The accessibility layer spans every state — keyboard, focus, and screen reader must hold across all of them.
The invariant: package the flow so it fails visibly under review, not silently in production.

design-review-packet.code:
# UX State, Accessibility & Review Packet

## Context
- Flow: submit an insurance claim (high-friction, multi-step form)
- Constraint: release risk — cannot ship a flow keyboard/SR users can't complete
- Assumption: most drop-off happens at the error + resubmit step

## State Inventory
| State     | System status shown | Primary action        | Notes |
|-----------|--------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| loading   | spinner + 'Saving' | none (disabled)       | aria-busy=true |
| empty     | 'No claims yet'    | 'Start a claim'       | first-run guidance |
| error     | field-level + banner | 'Fix & resubmit'    | focus moves to first error |
| disabled  | greyed, aria-disabled | tooltip 'why'       | reason is stated |
| success   | confirmation + ref# | 'View claim'         | the demoed screen |

## Accessibility (WCAG)
- [ ] keyboard-only: full flow reachable, no traps  (hook: keyboard-only walkthrough)
- [ ] focus order: DOM order matches visual order; error moves focus
- [ ] screen reader: labels + error text announced  (hook: screen-reader smoke pass)
- [ ] contrast: error red passes 4.5:1  (hook: axe accessibility scan)

## Selected vs Rejected
- Selected: inline field errors + focus-to-first-error
- Rejected: single top banner only — SR users never hear which field

## Expected Failure & Repair
- Failure: on submit error, focus stays on the button; SR user hears nothing
- Repair: move focus to first invalid field, aria-live=assertive on the summary

## Before/After Critique
- Before: error banner appears off-screen, no focus move, context lost
- After: focus + announcement + inline messages; recovery in one step

## Reviewer Objection
- 'Is this proven or just described?' -> attached axe report + keyboard GIF

## Evidence
- axe_scan.json · keyboard_walkthrough.md · usability_prompt.md

steps.label: Context + the real constraint
steps.note: Name the flow and that the operating constraint is release/review risk — not aesthetics. State the assumption you're testing so a reviewer knows what to attack.

steps.label: The state inventory
steps.note: Every row is a state a demo skips. 'System status shown' is the heuristic that catches hidden loading/disabled states; the error row's focus-move note is the recovery hinge.

steps.label: WCAG checklist with hooks named
steps.note: Each line binds to a concrete inspection hook (axe scan, keyboard-only walkthrough, screen-reader smoke pass). A checkbox with no hook output is a wish, not proof.

steps.label: Selected vs rejected
steps.note: The rejected option (top-banner-only) is the one that looks acceptable in review and fails for screen-reader users — the exact invalidation condition.

steps.label: Expected failure + repair
steps.note: The realistic failure: focus stranded on the submit button after an error. The repair is specific and testable, not 'improve accessibility'.

steps.label: Reviewer objection + evidence
steps.note: Pre-answer 'proven or described?' by attaching the axe report and keyboard walkthrough. The evidence line is what makes the packet inspectable.
